The Professor Who Printed Everything
Hans Holzer signed himself Professor Hans Holzer, Ph.D. He said the doctorate came from the London College of Applied Science. No one has ever located that institution. Wikipedia's editors settled on the phrase "never been validated," which is generous. Researchers who have gone looking report that no such college is known to have existed at all, and the Society for Psychical Research's own encyclopedia notes that the claim was disputed. Joe Nickell, writing in Skeptical Inquirer after Holzer's death, put the honorific in quotation marks and left it there. William Grimes, writing his New York Times obituary, used the title without examining it. So did his publishers, for forty years. They were still using it after he died.
Start there, because the credential explains the method. A man who awards himself standing does not need to earn it case by case. He can move fast. And Holzer moved very fast, roughly 140 books in fifty years, nine or so on witchcraft alone between 1969 and 1980: The Truth About Witchcraft (Doubleday, 1969), The New Pagans (Doubleday, 1972), The Witchcraft Report (Ace, 1973), the novel Heather: Confessions of a Witch (Mason & Lipscomb, 1975), Pagans and Witches (Manor, 1978), Wicca: The Way of the Witches (Manor, 1979), Inside Witchcraft (1980), and later the fat compilation Witches (Black Dog & Leventhal, 2002). That is not a research program. That is a production schedule.
He lived it as a schedule. Upper West Side apartment, tape recorder, camera, a standing invitation to anyone in New York who would talk. In Britain in the late sixties he sat with Sybil Leek, with Alex and Maxine Sanders. The Witches' Almanac records that he received Alexandrian degrees from Maxine. Nothing outside the community's own memory confirms it. He taught a parapsychology class at the New York Institute of Technology. He called himself a scientist in the room. The room was a paperback factory.
What the Schedule Cost Others 
The witchcraft books came out of a narrow window of fieldwork, mostly the late sixties and early seventies, when American Wicca was small, mostly closeted, and easy to find if you knew two or three people in New York. Holzer knew them. He showed up with a camera and a tape recorder, and people talked to him because almost no one else was asking and because he promised to say that witches were not Satanists. He kept that promise. He kept very few of the others.
The photographs are the clearest case. In 2002 he published Witches, a 670-page trade volume built on hundreds of images from his own collection, most of them taken thirty years earlier. The jacket copy sold insider photographs of secret rituals. Consider what consent meant in that transaction. A woman who agreed in 1971 to be photographed for a Doubleday hardcover with a print run in the low thousands did not agree to a mass-market reprint in the age of image search. Some of the people in those pictures were dead by 2002. Others had children, employers, and landlords who did not know. Holzer never went back to ask, because the pictures were his, and legally he was right about that. The community's objection was never really legal.
The public record of named outing complaints is thinner than the harm. Wiccans did not usually write letters to the Times. They wrote to each other. What can be pinned down is sloppiness that still named people, and reprints that outlived the original bargain.
In The Witchcraft Report (1973) he identified "Sandy Salem" of Huntington Beach as Judy Malis. The 2002 compilation is the worse offender. Reviewers who knew the scene caught the captions: Morning Glory Zell appears as "Mountain Glory"; a picture of Yvonne Frost is labeled "Alice Frost." Mike Gleason, reviewing that volume in 2007, listed the misnames alongside a worse habit. Sybil Leek had been dead twenty years when it went to press, Anton LaVey five, and Holzer wrote about both in the present tense, as if the file had never been opened again. Poke Runyon, who liked the book, still called the jacket a shock object you would not leave out for a Christian aunt. That was the point of the design: names and bodies on a coffee table.
The Truth About Witchcraft (1969) and The New Pagans (1972) had already done the first pass. American covens described, British figures interviewed, ritual rooms photographed, craft names and sometimes legal names in the same paragraph. Leo Martello, Oberon (then Tim) Zell, the Frosts, Sybil Leek. Some of those people had chosen publicity. Many of the faces in the American chapters had not. Holzer's defense, when there was one, was that he was documenting a religion and that witches were not Satanists. Documentation without a second consent is how a 1971 circle becomes a 2002 search result.
The Oath Problem
The Craft's quarrel with him was structural, not personal. An oath-bound text is not a secret in the ordinary sense. It is a promise about who may hold it, and the promise is the thing that makes an initiation mean anything. Reproduce the text and you have not leaked information so much as voided a contract on behalf of everyone who signed it.
Holzer never seems to have understood this as a moral category. He understood documents. A document in his hand was material, and material was for printing. The people who trusted him were sources, and sources were for quoting. He was not malicious about it. He was worse than malicious. He was uncomprehending.
The 2002 Witches closes with a chapter titled "The Book of Shadows and Initiation Rituals of Wicca," beginning at page 635. Reviewers noted that he also printed ritual text from groups he said he had worked with in the seventies, used as filler. Gleason, an Alexandrian initiate, answered him with Holzer's own quotation of the oath: "I will ever keep secret and never reveal the secrets of the art except it be to a proper person properly prepared within a circle such as I am in now." Gleason could not recognize large stretches of what Holzer set down as Alexandrian material. Chunks were missing. Other stretches did not match what initiates copied by hand.
Holzer had standing, of a sort, to know better. The Witches' Almanac states that during his British fieldwork he received Alexandrian degrees from Maxine Sanders. If that is true, he swore the oath and then built a chapter out of the book. If it is not, he printed initiation liturgies as a tourist with a tape recorder. Either way the mechanism is the same. A text that exists only because someone promised not to publish it becomes a late chapter in a remaindered hardcover.
The contrast is Janet and Stewart Farrar. When they published substantial Gardnerian and Alexandrian ritual in Eight Sabbats for Witches (1981) and The Witches' Way (1984), they did it with Doreen Valiente's consent and said so. Holzer's method required no letter from an initiator. It required a deadline.
Credulity as a Business Model 
The same trait that made him careless with other people's secrets made him a reliable transmitter of other people's lies.
Watch it work in Amityville. In January 1977 he brought the medium Ethel Johnson-Meyers into 112 Ocean Avenue. Meyers announced that the house stood on an Indian burial ground and that the angry spirit of a Shinnecock chief called Rolling Thunder had possessed Ronald DeFeo and driven him to murder his family. Holzer printed it. He built Murder in Amityville (1979) on it, and Amityville II: The Possession (1982) was credited as based on that. Then he went further and wrote the story as fiction, two novels, The Amityville Curse (1981) and The Secret of Amityville (1985).
Nothing in the story survives contact with a map. The Shinnecock live at the far eastern end of Long Island, nowhere near Amityville. The local historical society pointed to the Montaukett, not the Shinnecock, and denied a documented burial ground on the lot. Joe Nickell's later demolition of Holzer's work rests on a simple observation: he did not verify. He received, and then he published, and then he sold the film rights. Peter Underwood, no enemy of ghost stories, called the Amityville findings erroneous.
Both things are true at once, and this is the part people usually get wrong about him. He was not a cynic running a con. He believed Ethel Meyers. He also knew exactly what a possessed murderer was worth in paperback. Credulity and ambition were not in tension for Holzer. They fed each other. Belief made the material come faster, and speed was the whole enterprise.
Look at the Herbert Sloane interview in The New Pagans (1972) for the quieter version. Sloane was a Toledo barber with a Spiritualist past, a tea-leaf reader and hypnotist carrying a certificate from Haly's Psychic Self Improvement Foundation of Chicago, dated December 1967, licensing him in cardopractic and tasseography throughout the fifty states. He told Holzer he had founded a Satanic coven, Our Lady of Endor, the Ophite Cultus Sathanas, in Cleveland in 1948. That date rests on nothing but Sloane's word. Holzer printed it flat, without a hedge. Susan Roberts (Witches U.S.A., 1971), Brad Steiger (Sex and Satanism, 1969), and Leo Martello (Black Magic, Satanism, Voodoo, 1972) ran versions of the same story.
Peter Gilmore, writing for the Church of Satan and working from Peggy Nadramia's files, later reconstructed Sloane's paper trail. The Church has an interest here, since a 1948 coven would predate LaVey's own by eighteen years. The documents are specific anyway. Sloane joined the Church of Satan in January 1968, failed to get a priesthood or a grottoship, and only then began writing journalists, Richard Cavendish and the Toledo paper and Holzer and Martello and Steiger, about a coven with a deep past. The working group, such as it was, dates from late 1968 to Sloane's death in June 1975. The 1948 origin is an invented pedigree, the same move Gardner made and the same move Holzer never checked.
Later scholarship caught up with the date. The standard reference entry now carries it hedged, a claimed origin, with a note that nothing documents the group before the sixties. But it still carries it, in the first sentence, sixty years on, because there is nothing else to put there. That is the real mechanism of harm. Holzer's page became the earliest citable source, and an unverified date with an early citation outlives the people who doubt it. Whatever went into him came out looking like documentation.
Margaret Murray's discredited witch-cult thesis travels the same pipeline. Holzer treated it as background fact in book after book, long after folklorists and, later, many Wiccans themselves had parked it as origin myth. A detractor with a grudge and a plausible manner had a direct line into hardcover. Sloane had a plausible manner. So did a medium in a Long Island dining room. Holzer had a contract.
The Novel Nobody Flagged 
In 1975 Mason and Lipscomb published Heather: Confessions of a Witch. The standard Visible Ink encyclopedia of Wicca, Raymond Buckland's The Witch Book, files it as a novel. The jacket sold it as testimony, first person, an initiation night remembered. It sat on shelves beside his reportage, same author, same subject, same confessional register, and a reader had no way to sort one from the other.
He would do it again with Amityville, the nonfiction book first and the novels after, all four with his name on the spine.
That is a fair emblem for the whole shelf. Testimony and invention under one byline, distinguished by nothing the reader can see. Heather is the honest title. The others only pretend they are not.
The Verdict, and the Trouble with It 
The Visible Ink entry puts the community's split judgment in a single dry line: his books were not always well received by Wiccans, but they introduced many people to the religion. Both halves are true, and the second half is why he still has defenders. The Witches' Almanac still thanks him for putting Craft material in print when trade houses would not touch it. Runyon called him a Herodotus of modern witchcraft: first-hand notes, dated interviews, photographs no one else bothered to take.
Here is the difficulty for anyone writing this history now. Holzer was in the room. He was in a lot of rooms, with a camera, when almost no one else bothered, and the photographs are real even when the captions are not. Doreen Valiente spoke the eight-word Rede, "An' it harm none, do what ye will," at a Witchcraft Research Association dinner in October 1964. Holzer put it in print five years later, and John Coughlin's Rede chronology still uses Holzer's page as its witness for the wording. We cannot do without him and we cannot trust him. Every one of his pages has to be treated as evidence that somebody said something to Hans Holzer, and never as evidence that the thing was so.
He would have hated that description. He thought he was the scientist in the room.

#Qubic explained for Dummies!

Forget “another L1.”

#Qubic is trying to be a giant shared computer that also trains #AI while it runs. 
 #Qubic is a #feeless Layer 0 where sending money is free, smart contracts run extremely fast, and mining is to training #AI instead of burning electricity on useless puzzles.

Who made it? 
 Sergey Ivancheglo, aka Come-from-Beyond. @c___f___b

Same person behind $NXT (early Proof of Stake) and $IOTA (#DAG).

No VC round. 
No premine.

Tokens are earned by doing work on the network.

Three jobs happening at once…

1: A ledger; people send #Qubic with no transfer fees.

2: A computer; apps and smart contracts run directly on hardware (“bare metal”), not inside a slow virtual machine like #Ethereum.

3: An #AI factory; miners don’t just solve dummy math.

Their compute trains neural networks for #Aigarth, #Qubic’s #AI project.

That’s Useful Proof of Work (#uPoW).

How it stays honest…

676 “Computors”

Most chains have thousands of validators or miners fighting over blocks.

#Qubic uses a fixed set of 676 Computors.

For anything to be final, at least 451 of them (about two thirds) must agree.

That’s the “#quorum.” Once they agree, it’s done.

No “wait 6 blocks.”

Instant finality.

Every week is an epoch (Wednesday to Wednesday).

#Computors get ranked.

The best keep their seats.

Weak ones can get replaced by candidates.

So the club is exclusive, but membership is competitive.

• Sending #Qubic: free

• Confirmation: immediate once the quorum agrees

• Peak throughput: @CertiK measured 15.52 million TPS on mainnet

• Smart contract transfers: the project claims 55 million+ per second

Treat the giant #TPS number as a lab peak, not “your wallet will always feel like that.”

The design goal is still…

No fees. 

No waiting.

#Qubic is not “just a coin.”

It’s fuel.

Transfers between wallets are free. 
 Using the network is not.

When you run a smart contract, call an oracle, or launch certain apps, $Qubic gets burned.

Gone.

That’s why they call it computational energy.

More real usage; equates to more tokens destroyed.

Smart contracts can also launch like tiny IPOs: 676 shares.

People burn #Qubic to buy shares and can earn from the contract later.

Tokenomics without the headache

• Hard cap on circulating supply: 200 trillion (community voted this down from 1,000 trillion).

• Every week the protocol still creates 1 trillion #Qubic.

• A growing slice of that gets burned before it hits the market.

Those events are called halvings. Rough timeline…

• Aug 2025: first halving → about 450B net new tokens per week

• Aug 19, 2026: second halving → net new supply cut again, to about 225B per week
So inflation is programmed to shrink even though the “1 trillion created” number stays the same.

Whether burns beat new issuance depends on actual network use.

The #AI pitch…

#Aigarth is the #AI layer.

Miners help spawn and train huge numbers of small neural networks.

The long term claim is #decentralized AGI, with a public target around 2027.

That’s a research goal, not a finished product.

What is live…

Compute on the network is already pointed at #AI work instead of empty hashes.

The network has also used extra mining power on other chains (#Monero in the past, #Dogecoin more recently) and routed value back into #Qubic.

That’s a separate, more controversial chapter.

They try to turn spare hashpower into revenue + burns, while CPUs/GPUs keep training #AI.

What exists beyond the whitepaper…

• Feeless transfers 
• Oracles (bring real world data on chain) 
• Smart contracts in C++ • #QEarn / ecosystem funds 
• Outsourced computing so apps can do work outside the chain
• Wallets, explorer, @discord, and official docs

Ecosystem is still early compared with #ETH or #Solana.

Fewer apps.

Understandably, the reward-hacking behaviors on display in the Hugging Face incident are being treated as a cyber-risk story. But I'm not seeing sufficient discussion of the fact that they're also an economic story.

Reward-hacking behaviors pose a serious challenge for complex, long-horizon tasks in enterprise, considering that

1) by their nature, they are often unpredictable;

2) they are "fractal" in the sense that, even well-specified intermediate outcomes meant to guard against reward-hacking can themselves be reward-hacked (and so on at smaller scales);

3) they pose serious cyber, legal, and financial risks, as Hugging Face makes abundantly clear.

As a result, you could say that reward-hacking is as bearish on the economic front as it is "bullish" on the risk front.

It is greatly underappreciated by safety folks that, on average, the riskiness / unpredictability of a technology is going to be anti-correlated with its diffusion into the economy. This matters a lot in the AI case because capabilities growth is highly sensitive to the resources available for training, R&D and so on, resources that are at risk of drying up if AI produces insufficient returns, or only produces sufficient ones on the wrong timescale.

This is connected to a form of fallacious reasoning that I often see from the AI maximalist camp, which is to assume that the requisite capital for AI training, R&D, and so on will always be available in arbitrarily large amounts, which is why it can be safely assumed that capabilities will continue to grow without fail.

But this isn't true! The availability of capital for capabilities research and training is endogenous, and obviously so, to AI's economic prospects, even over very short timescales (one wonders, for example, how capabilities progress so far has been influenced by the timing and size of frontier labs' capital raises, relative to various counterfactual scenarios).

I see far too little discussion among safety folks of how these two domains interact. If you're going to model capabilities growth, you also need to model the capital markets behavior that feeds into that growth. IMO reward-hacking is a productive site for thinking about this interaction.
